## Christ the Mediator: What the 1689 London Baptist Confession Teaches

The 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith dedicates a significant portion of its eighth chapter to the person and work of Christ, specifically focusing on his role as Mediator. Here's a breakdown of the key teachings, organized for clarity:

**I. His Divine and Human Natures (Paragraphs 1-3)**

* **Truly God & Truly Man (Paragraph 1):** The Confession firmly establishes the hypostatic union – that Jesus Christ is *both* fully God and fully man, united in one person. He is not merely a man empowered by God, nor is he a lesser God. He is the eternal Son of God, who took on human nature. This is crucial for his mediatorial work.
* **God from Eternity (Paragraph 2):**  Christ is "God from eternity, being of the same substance, majesty, and glory with the Father." This highlights his pre-existence and inherent deity.  He didn't *become* God, he *is* God.
* **Man of the Substance of His Mother (Paragraph 3):**  He took on human nature, being "made of the substance of his Mother," being conceived by the Holy Spirit. He is truly human, with a real body and soul, subject to all human limitations (except sin).  This is vital for representing humanity before God.

**II. His Offices as Mediator (Paragraphs 4-8)**

The Confession outlines three primary offices of Christ as Mediator: Prophet, Priest, and King.

* **Prophet (Paragraph 4):** Christ is the ultimate Prophet, revealing God's will and purpose. He doesn't just *speak* for God, he *is* the Word of God. He reveals truth through his teachings, miracles, and ultimately, through the inspired scriptures. He perfectly declares God’s will.
* **Priest (Paragraphs 5-7):** This is the most extensively covered office.
    * **Appointed by God (Paragraph 5):** Christ was appointed by God to be the High Priest of our profession. This appointment wasn't earned, but given by the Father.
    * **Offering Himself as a Sacrifice (Paragraph 6):**  His priestly work centers on offering *himself* as a perfect sacrifice for the sins of his people. This sacrifice is both a propitiation (satisfying God's wrath) and an expiation (covering our sins).  It's a *finished* work, meaning it doesn't need to be repeated.
    * **Intercession (Paragraph 7):**  Christ continually intercedes for his people in heaven, presenting their needs and righteousness to the Father. This intercession is based on the merit of his finished work. He doesn’t *ask* for mercy, but *claims* it based on the satisfaction he provided.
* **King (Paragraph 8):** Christ is the King of his Church, appointed by God to govern and defend his people. His kingdom is spiritual, not earthly (though it has earthly implications). He exercises his kingship through his Word and Spirit, subduing the enemies of his kingdom.  His reign will ultimately be fully realized at his second coming.

**III. The Extent of His Mediation (Paragraph 9)**

* **For the Elect Only:** This is a crucial and often debated point. The Confession states that Christ's mediation is *effective* only for those whom God has predestined to salvation – the elect. While his sacrifice is *sufficient* for all, it is *efficient* only for those who believe.  This doesn't mean Christ *willed* all to be saved, but that God the Father chose a people for whom Christ would actually secure salvation.
* **Not Universal Redemption:** The Confession rejects the idea of universal redemption, arguing that if Christ died for all equally, then none would certainly be saved.  His death secures salvation for those given to him by the Father.



**IV.  His Humiliation and Exaltation (Paragraphs 10-12)**

* **Humiliation (Paragraph 10):** The Confession details Christ's humiliation – his voluntary emptying of himself (Philippians 2:7), taking on the form of a servant, and suffering the curse of the law for sinners. This includes his suffering in his life, his death on the cross, and his burial.
* **Resurrection (Paragraph 11):** His resurrection is central. He rose again on the third day, demonstrating his victory over sin and death, and validating his claims.
* **Exaltation (Paragraph 12):**  He is now exalted at the right hand of God, reigning in glory, and awaiting the time when he will return to judge the living and the dead.




**Key Takeaways:**

* **Christ's dual nature is essential:**  His deity makes his sacrifice infinite in value, and his humanity makes it possible for him to represent us.
* **His mediatorial work is complete and finished:**  He doesn't need to be repeatedly sacrificed.
* **His mediation is effective for the elect:**  This is a defining feature of the Confession's soteriology (doctrine of salvation).
* **His offices are interconnected:**  His prophetic, priestly, and kingly roles work together to accomplish salvation.




You can find the full text of the 1689 London Baptist Confession here: [https://www.1689confession.org/](https://www.1689confession.org/)  (specifically Chapter 8)



It's important to note that interpretations of the Confession, particularly regarding the extent of the atonement, can vary within Baptist circles.  However, the above represents the core teachings of the Confession on the person and work of Christ as Mediator.

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about effectual calling?
questions.reference_answer: Those whom God hath predestinated unto Life, he is pleased in his appointed, and accepted time, effectually to call by his word, and Spirit, out of that state of sin, and death, in which they are by nature, to grace and Salvation by Jesus Christ; inlightning their minds, spiritually, and savingly to understand the things of God; taking away their heart of stone, and giving unto them an heart of flesh; renewing their wills, and by his Almighty power determining them to that which is good, and effectually drawing them to Jesus Christ; yet so as they come most freely, being made willing by his Grace. This Effectual Call is of God's free, and special grace alone, not from any thing at all foreseen in man, nor from any power, or agency in the Creature, coworking with his special Grace, the Creature being wholly passive therein, being dead in sins and trespasses, until being quickned & renewed by the holy Spirit, he is thereby enabled to answer this call, and to embrace the Grace offered and conveyed in it; and that by no less power, then that which raised up Christ from the dead. Elect Infants dying in infancy, are regenerated and saved by Christ through the Spirit; who worketh when, and where, and how he pleaseth: so also are all other elect persons, who are uncapable of being outwardly called by the Ministry of the Word. Others not elected, although they may be called by the Ministry of the word, and may have some common operations of the Spirit, yet not being effectually drawn by the Father, they neither will, nor can truly come to Christ; and therefore cannot be saved: much less can men that receive not the Christian Religion be saved; be they never so diligent to frame their lives according to the light of nature, and the Law of that Religion they do profess.

The 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith has a substantial section on effectual calling, found in **Chapter X, "Of Free Will."** It's a crucial doctrine for Baptists, emphasizing God's sovereign initiative in salvation while also acknowledging human responsibility. Here's a breakdown of what it teaches, broken down into key points with references to the relevant paragraphs:

**1. God's Sovereign Initiative (Paragraph 1-3):**

* **God's Will is Supreme:** The Confession firmly states that God is the ultimate cause of salvation.  It rejects any notion that humans can initiate their own salvation.  "God having decreed to save some men, and to leave others to perish, according to his pleasure..." (X.1). This is a strong statement of divine sovereignty.
* **Man's Natural Inability:**  Humans, by nature, are unable to turn to God on their own.  "Man, in his fallen state, hath no power to turn to God of himself, nor to choose the things that are spiritually good..." (X.2).  The Confession emphasizes the total depravity of humanity – we are dead in sin and unable to respond to God positively without divine intervention.
* **Effectual Calling is God's Work:**  Effectual calling is *entirely* the work of God.  "It is the free and special grace of God, which he hath been pleased to extend to those who are chosen to salvation, that he doth powerfully and effectually call them..." (X.4).  This isn't merely an outward offer of salvation, but a powerful, internal work.

**2. The Nature of Effectual Calling (Paragraph 4-5):**

* **Operation of the Holy Spirit:** Effectual calling is specifically the work of the Holy Spirit.  "The Spirit of God works when and where, and how, and upon whom he pleases..." (X.4).  He doesn't work according to human merit or seeking, but according to His sovereign will.
* **Internal and Powerful:**  It's not simply an external invitation, but an internal, transformative work.  "...by his own power, doth overcome the natural aversion of man, and incline him to, and enable him to accept the offers of mercy in Christ." (X.4).  The Spirit doesn't just *inform* the will, but *inclines* and *enables* it.
* **Irresistible (but not coercive):** This is a key, and often debated, point. The Confession doesn't use the word "irresistible" directly, but the language strongly implies it. The Spirit *overcomes* aversion and *enables* acceptance.  While God doesn't *force* a person to believe against their will (coercion), the work of the Spirit is so powerful that those He calls *will* believe.  It's not that they *can* resist, but that they *won't* ultimately resist.
* **Not all are Called Effectually:**  The Confession clearly states that not everyone who hears the gospel is effectually called.  "Unto those that are ordained to eternal life, God doth grant faith, and repentance, so as they may come unto him..." (X.5).  This reinforces the doctrine of election.

**3.  The Result of Effectual Calling (Paragraph 5-6):**

* **Faith and Repentance are Gifts:** Faith and repentance are not things humans generate themselves, but are *granted* by God as a result of effectual calling.  "Unto those that are ordained to eternal life, God doth grant faith, and repentance, so as they may come unto him..." (X.5).
* **Voluntary Obedience:**  While faith and repentance are gifts, the Confession also emphasizes that obedience is *voluntary*. "...and that voluntarily, and joyfully, they obey his will." (X.5).  This is important to avoid the charge of determinism.  The called person *wants* to obey because God has changed their heart.
* **Distinction from Common Grace:** The Confession distinguishes effectual calling from the "common grace" of God, which restrains evil and offers the gospel to all.  Effectual calling is a *special* grace given only to the elect.



**In essence, the 1689 London Baptist Confession teaches that effectual calling is a sovereign, internal, and powerful work of the Holy Spirit that overcomes human resistance and enables those chosen by God to willingly and joyfully believe in and obey Jesus Christ.**  It's a doctrine that highlights God's initiative in salvation while still affirming human responsibility (though that responsibility is only possible *because* of God's prior work).



You can find the full text of the Confession here: [https://www.1689confession.com/](https://www.1689confession.com/)  (specifically Chapter X).



It's worth noting that interpretations of "irresistible grace" within Baptist circles can vary.  Some emphasize the power of the Spirit to overcome resistance, while others stress the voluntary nature of the response.  However, the Confession's overall emphasis is clearly on God's sovereign control in the calling of His people.

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about justification?
questions.reference_answer: Those whom God Effectually calleth, he also freely justifieth, not by infusing Righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting, and accepting their Persons as Righteous; not for any thing wrought in them, or done by them, but for Christ's sake alone, not by imputing faith it self, the act of beleiving, or any other evangelical obedience to them, as their Righteousness; but by imputing Christs active obedience unto the whole Law, and passive obedience in his death, for their whole and sole Righteousnnss, they receiving, and resting on him, and his Righteousness, by Faith; which faith they have not of themselves, it is the gift of God. Faith thus receiving and resting on Christ, and his Righteousness, is the alone instrument of Justification: yet it is not alone in the person justified, but is ever accompanied with all other saving Graces, and is no dead faith, but worketh by love. Christ by his obedience, and death, did fully discharge the debt of all those that are justified; and did by the sacrifice of himself, in the blood of his cross, undergoing in their stead, the penalty due unto them: make a proper, real and full satisfaction to Gods justice in their behalf: yet in asmuch as he was given by the Father for them, and his Obedience and Satisfaction accepted in their stead, and both freely, not for any thing in them; their Justification is only of Free Grace, that both the exact justice and rich Grace of God, might be glorified in the Justification of sinners. God did from all eternity decreeto justifie all the Elect, and Christ did in the fulness of time die for their sins, and rise again for their Justification; Nevertheless they are not justified personally, untill the Holy Spirit, doth in due time actually apply Christ unto them. God doth continue to Forgive the sins of those that are justified, and although they can never fall from the state of justication; yet they may by their sins fall under Gods Fatherly displeasure; and in that condition, they have not usually the light of his Countenance restored unto them, untill they humble themselves, confess their sins, beg pardon, and renew their faith, and repentance. The Justification of Believers under the Old Testament was in all these respects, one and the same with the justification of Believers under the New Tement.

The 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith has a substantial section dedicated to Justification, found in **Chapter 10: Of Free Justification**. Here's a breakdown of its key teachings on the subject, categorized for clarity.  It's a fairly detailed and nuanced treatment, deeply rooted in Reformed theology.  I'll also include references to the specific paragraphs within the chapter.

**1. The Definition of Justification (Paragraph 1)**

* **Not Making Righteous:** Justification is *not* making a sinner righteous in themselves. It doesn't change their inherent corruption. It's not an infusion of righteousness *into* the believer.
* **An Act of God's Free Grace:** It's an act of God's free grace, not something earned or merited by human works.
* **Declaring Righteous:** It's God *declaring* a sinner righteous in His sight.  This declaration is based on the righteousness of Christ.
* **Legal Declaration:** It's a forensic (legal) act – a judicial declaration, not an internal transformation (though that *follows* justification through sanctification).

**2. The Basis of Justification: Christ's Righteousness (Paragraphs 1-2)**

* **Perfect Obedience & Suffering:** The sole basis for justification is the perfect obedience and suffering of Jesus Christ. His righteousness is *imputed* (credited) to the believer.
* **Active & Passive Obedience:**  The Confession emphasizes both Christ's *active obedience* (perfectly keeping the law) and His *passive obedience* (suffering the penalty for sin).  Both are necessary to satisfy divine justice.
* **Not Our Own Righteousness:**  Our own works, even those done *after* conversion, are not the ground of our justification. They are evidence *of* justification, but not the cause.
* **Complete Righteousness:**  Christ's righteousness is a *complete* righteousness, fully satisfying the demands of God's law.

**3. How Justification is Received: Faith (Paragraphs 3-4)**

* **Instrumental Cause:** Faith is the *instrument* by which we receive Christ's righteousness. It's not the *cause* of justification, but the means through which it's applied.
* **Not a Work:** Faith is not a work done *by* us that merits justification. It is itself a gift of God (Ephesians 2:8-9).
* **Accepting Christ & His Righteousness:** Faith involves receiving, resting upon, and relying on Christ alone for salvation.  It's a trusting acceptance of His righteousness.
* **Seeing Christ as Prophet, Priest, and King:** True faith includes a seeing of Christ in all His offices – as the prophet who reveals God’s will, the priest who makes atonement, and the king who reigns over us.

**4. The Effects of Justification (Paragraphs 5-7)**

* **Peace with God:** Justification brings peace with God, removing His wrath and displeasure.
* **Pardon of Sin:**  All sins – past, present, and future – are pardoned through justification. (This is a point of some nuance; the Confession also affirms the need for confession of sin after conversion).
* **Adoption into God's Family:**  Believers are adopted as children of God, receiving all the privileges of sonship.
* **Inheritance of Eternal Life:** Justification secures our inheritance of eternal life.
* **Union with Christ:** Justification is closely linked to union with Christ.  We are united to Him, and His righteousness becomes ours.
* **Not a License to Sin:** Justification does *not* lead to licentiousness (a license to sin). True faith produces good works as evidence of a changed life.  (Paragraph 6 specifically addresses this concern).
* **Certainty (Though Sometimes Obscured):** While assurance of justification can be obscured by doubts, the Confession affirms that true believers *are* certainly justified in God’s sight. (Paragraph 7).  It acknowledges the possibility of falling into doubt, but emphasizes that the grace of Christ is sufficient to overcome those doubts.



**Key Theological Emphases:**

* **Sola Christus (Christ Alone):** Justification is entirely based on the work of Christ.
* **Sola Gratia (Grace Alone):** Justification is a free gift of God's grace, not earned by human merit.
* **Sola Fide (Faith Alone):**  Faith is the *instrument* of receiving justification, though not the cause.
* **Forensic Justification:**  The Confession strongly emphasizes the *legal* or *forensic* nature of justification – a declaration of righteousness in God's court.



**Where to find the full text:**

You can read the full 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith here:  [https://www.1689confession.org/](https://www.1689confession.org/)



In summary, the 1689 LBCF presents a robust and biblically grounded understanding of justification as a legal declaration by God, based solely on the imputed righteousness of Jesus Christ, and received by faith. It's a central doctrine within the Confession, shaping its understanding of salvation and the relationship between God and humanity.

questions.question: What does the 1689 London Baptist Confession teach about the perseverance of the saints?
questions.reference_answer: Those whom God hath accepted in the beloved, effectually called and Sanctified by his Spirit, and given the precious faith of his Elect unto, can neither totally nor finally fall from the state of grace; but shall certainly persevere therein to the end and be eternally saved, seeing the gifts and callings of God are without Repentance, (whence he still begets and nourisheth in them Faith, Repentance, Love, Joy, Hope, and all the graces of the Spirit unto immortality) and though many storms and floods arise and beat against them, yet they shall never be able to take them off that foundation and rock which by faith they are fastned upon: notwithstanding through unbelief and the temptations of Satan the sensible sight of the light and love of God, may for a time be clouded, and obscured from them, yet he is still the same and they shall be sure to be kept by the power of God unto Salvation, where they shall enjoy their purchased possession, they being engraven upon the palm of his hands, and their names having been written in the book of life from all Eternity. This perseverance of the Saints depends not upon their own free will; but upon the immutability of the decree of Election flowing from the free and unchangeable love of God the Father; upon the efficacy of the merit and intercession of Jesus Christ and Union with him, the oath of God, the abiding of his Spirit & the seed of God within them, and the nature of the Covenant of Grace from all which ariseth also the certainty and infallibility thereof. And though they may through the temptation of Satan and of the world, the prevalency of corruption remaining in them, and the neglect of means of their preservation fall into grievous sins, and for a time continue therein; whereby they incur Gods displeasure, and grieve his holy Spirit, come to have their graces and comforts impaired have their hearts hardened, and their Consciences wounded, hurt, and scandalize others, and bring temporal judgements upon themselves: yet they shall renew their repentance and be preserved through faith in Christ Jesus to the end.

The 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith has a substantial section dedicated to the Perseverance of the Saints (Chapter 10, "Of Free Justification"). Here's a breakdown of what it teaches, broken down into key points and with relevant quotes:

**Core Doctrine: True Believers *Will* Persevere**

The central tenet is that those who are truly regenerated by God's Spirit and justified by faith *will* persevere in grace and never fall away from that state to final perdition. This isn't based on their own strength, but on God's sovereign power and unchanging love.

* **Paragraph 1:** "They who are effectually called, and truly regenerated, shall never wholly nor finally fall away from the state of grace, but shall certainly persevere therein to the end, and be eternally saved."  This is the foundational statement.  It's a definite assertion of "once saved, always saved" – though the Confession frames it in terms of God's preserving power rather than simply a one-time decision.

**Reasons for Perseverance (God's Work, Not Ours)**

The Confession doesn't attribute perseverance to the believer's willpower or consistent good works. Instead, it grounds it in the work of God:

* **God's Decree & Election (Paragraph 1):** Perseverance is rooted in God's eternal decree and election.  Those chosen by God *will* be preserved.
* **God's Powerful Preservation (Paragraph 1):**  "This perseverance of the saints depends upon the effectual working of the Spirit of Christ within them: who will never suffer them to fall totally from grace, but will preserve them by his power, to the end."  The Holy Spirit is the active agent in keeping believers secure.
* **God's Unchanging Love (Paragraph 1):** "…and by his grace enable them to stand firm in the faith, and to continue in holiness, until their final glorification."  God's love isn't conditional on our performance; it's the basis for our preservation.
* **God's Covenant (Paragraph 4):**  The covenant of grace, established by God, guarantees this perseverance.



**Addressing Apparent Failures & Disciplining God's Children**

The Confession acknowledges that believers *will* sin and may even experience periods of doubt and spiritual darkness. However, these are not evidence of a loss of salvation.

* **Temporary Falls are Possible (Paragraph 2):** "True believers may, through the weakness of the flesh, and the temptations of Satan, fall into divers sins, and errors, and so grieve the Spirit, and lose a sense of God’s favour;…"  Believers *do* sin, and this is a normal part of the Christian life.
* **God's Discipline is Loving (Paragraph 2):**  “…but they shall not totally nor finally fall away; for the Spirit of Christ, who dwells in them, will enable them to repent of their sins, and to recover themselves out of their errors, and to return to a renewed obedience to God."  God disciplines His children, but this discipline is restorative, not punitive in the sense of losing salvation.  It's a sign of sonship, not rejection.
* **Assurance Can Fluctuate (Paragraph 3):**  "Though believers are assured that their salvation is eternal, yet they may be shaken, and their assurance may be clouded through temptation, and the working of their own corruptions;…"  Assurance isn't a constant, unwavering feeling. It can ebb and flow.  The *reality* of salvation doesn't change, even if our *feeling* of assurance does.
* **God's Promise is Sure (Paragraph 3):** “…but they are still preserved in Christ, and shall finally be delivered from all their afflictions."  Even in times of doubt, God remains faithful.




**What Perseverance *Isn't* (Important Clarifications)**

The Confession implicitly addresses potential misunderstandings:

* **Not License to Sin:**  Perseverance doesn't mean believers are free to live however they please.  The Confession consistently emphasizes the importance of holiness and obedience.  Falling into sin is a *result* of weakness, not a *proof* of lost salvation, but it *should* be grieved and repented of.
* **Not Passive Waiting:**  While God is the active agent in preservation, believers are called to actively pursue holiness and resist temptation.  The Spirit works *through* us, not *for* us in a way that bypasses our responsibility.
* **Not Based on Works:**  Perseverance isn't earned by consistent good works. It's a gift of God's grace.




**In Summary:**

The 1689 London Baptist Confession firmly affirms the perseverance of the saints as a doctrine rooted in God’s sovereign grace, powerful preservation, and unchanging love.  It acknowledges the reality of sin and doubt in the Christian life, but insists that true believers, secured by God’s promise, will ultimately persevere to the end and be eternally saved.  It's a robustly Calvinistic doctrine, emphasizing God’s initiative and faithfulness in keeping His people.



You can read the full text of Chapter 10 here: [https://www.1689confession.org/chapters/chapter-10](https://www.1689confession.org/chapters/chapter-10)

The end of Gods appointing this Day, is for the manifestation of the glory of his Mercy, in the Eternal Salvation of the Elect; and of his Justice in the Eternal damnation of the Reprobate, who are wicked and disobedient; for then shall the Righteous go into Everlasting Life, and receive that fulness of Joy, and Glory, with everlasting reward, in the presence of the Lord: but the wicked who know not God, and obey not the Gospel of Jesus Christ, shall be cast into Eternal torments, and punished with everlasting destruction, from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power. As Christ would have us to be certainly perswaded that there shall be a Day of judgement, both to deter all men from sin, and for the greater consolation of the godly, in their adversity; so will he have that day unknown to Men, that they may shake off all carnal security, and be always watchful, because they know not at what hour, the Lord will come; and may ever be prepared to say, Come Lord Jesus, Come quickly, Amen.

Okay, let's break down what the 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith teaches about the Last Judgment. It's a fairly detailed treatment, covering several aspects. Here's a comprehensive overview, organized for clarity, with chapter and paragraph references.  I'll also add some explanatory notes to help understand the context.

**Chapter 31: Of the Last Judgment**

This entire chapter is dedicated to the topic, so it's the primary source.  Here's a breakdown of the key points, summarized from the paragraphs within:

**1. The Certainty and Time of the Judgment (Paragraph 1)**

*   **Certainty:** The Confession firmly asserts the *certainty* of a final judgment. It states that "At the day of judgment, God will publicly and righteously judge the whole world, both righteous and wicked."  This isn't a maybe; it *will* happen.
*   **Personal Return of Christ:**  The judgment will be presided over by the Lord Jesus Christ, who will personally return in glory. This is linked to the resurrection of the dead.
*   **Time:** The Confession doesn't specify a precise date, but it's tied to the end of the current age and the consummation of all things.  It will occur *after* the resurrection.

**2. The Resurrection of the Dead (Paragraph 2)**

*   **General Resurrection:**  All people who have ever lived will be resurrected.  This is not a partial resurrection, but a universal one.
*   **Bodily Resurrection:**  The resurrection will be *bodily*.  This isn't just a spiritual thing; our physical bodies will be raised.  The Confession emphasizes that the same body that died will be raised again, though it will be transformed into a glorious, incorruptible form.  (This is a clear affirmation of the resurrection of the body, countering any purely spiritual interpretations).
*   **Order of Resurrection:** The righteous will be raised *first* and then, after a period, the wicked.  This is based on interpretations of Scripture (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17, 1 Corinthians 15).

**3. The Judge and the Standard of Judgment (Paragraph 3)**

*   **Jesus Christ as Judge:** Jesus Christ is the appointed Judge of all.  This is based on John 5:22, where the Father has given all judgment to the Son.
*   **The Word of God as the Rule:** The standard by which people will be judged is the *revealed Word of God*.  This means that people will be judged according to whether their lives and beliefs align with the teachings of Scripture.  This is a crucial point for Baptists, emphasizing the authority of the Bible.
*   **Conscience as a Witness:** While the Word is the ultimate standard, each person's conscience will also bear witness, acknowledging their deeds.

**4. The State of the Judged – The Righteous (Paragraph 4)**

*   **Acquittal and Reward:** The righteous (those who are justified by faith in Jesus Christ) will be acquitted (declared not guilty) and receive eternal life.
*   **Public Declaration of Approval:**  Their righteousness will be publicly acknowledged before all.  This is a vindication of God's grace and the efficacy of Christ's atonement.
*   **Inheritance of Eternal Glory:** They will enter into the possession of eternal glory and the enjoyment of God forever.  This includes the new heavens and the new earth.
*   **Absence of Condemnation:** Because their sins have been covered by Christ's sacrifice, they will not be condemned.

**5. The State of the Judged – The Wicked (Paragraph 5)**

*   **Condemnation and Punishment:** The wicked will be condemned to eternal punishment.  This punishment is just and righteous, being the consequence of their own choices and rejection of God's grace.
*   **Eternal Separation from God:** The punishment is described as a state of "everlasting separation from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power." This is the core of hell – not merely physical torment, but the ultimate loss of communion with God.
*   **Torment of Conscience:** The Confession also speaks of "the torment of conscience" as part of the punishment. This highlights the internal anguish that will accompany the realization of their guilt and the loss of hope.
*   **Justice of God Vindicated:** The condemnation of the wicked will demonstrate the justice and holiness of God.



**Key Theological Emphases & Context**

*   **Sovereignty of God:**  The Confession consistently emphasizes God's sovereignty in the judgment. He is the one who appoints the Judge, sets the standard, and ultimately carries out the judgment.
*   **Justification by Faith:** The fate of the righteous is directly tied to their justification by faith in Jesus Christ.  This is a central tenet of Baptist theology.
*   **Biblical Authority:** The Word of God is the ultimate standard for judgment, reinforcing the Confession's commitment to *Sola Scriptura* (Scripture alone).
*   **Real and Literal:** The Confession takes a very real and literal view of both the resurrection and the final judgment. It's not allegorical or symbolic.
*   **Particular Judgment vs. General Judgment:** The Confession doesn't explicitly address the concept of a "particular judgment" (judgment immediately after death for each individual). It focuses on the *general* and final judgment at the end of the age.  However, many within the 1689 Baptist tradition would hold to a degree of accountability immediately after death, even if the full reckoning occurs at the Last Judgment.



**Where to find it:**

You can read the full text of the 1689 London Baptist Confession of Faith here: [https://www.1689confession.com/](https://www.1689confession.com/)  (Chapter 31 is the relevant section).



I hope this detailed explanation is helpful!  Let me know if you have any other questions.
